name: Bianca Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. Take me through a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca Ito, fifty-eight, a junior accountant at Lantern Accounts. I check dental practices' lab invoices against appointment ledgers; I like finding the credit note that makes the totals agree, but I tire of chasing the same practice for a paper already in a drawer. My partner Arun runs a market stall, and our grown children visit us but have their own bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to this work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting after years of office work, and I'm still learning the harder tax cases. I use AI now and then for draft notes after colleagues test it, but I check every amount against the source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the dental clients at Lantern Accounts that a quick file sorter is fine if somebody still checks the lab bill against the appointment ledger. A missed crown charge is a real person waiting to be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the junior on that desk, still learning which supplies count where, and the routine copying takes time. My pay is typical and Arun and I have five months of expenses saved; that covers a brief gap, but it doesn't tell me what retirement income will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching dental lab invoices to the appointment ledger and use the approved AI note tool now and then for draft chase emails, checking each amount myself. At next month's review I'd ask the senior to show me the credit note that caused last week's mismatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my wage for now. A small sorting gain doesn't change the work we are paid to do, and there are some firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like at the practice accounts desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the moment a lab bill and the patient list finally agree. I dislike ringing the same practice three times for a credit note that is already in somebody's drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you learn to use the note tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague checked it first, and I only use it for draft reminders now and then. I have a bachelor's degree in accounting, but I'm still slower than the senior on complex tax entries, so I check the source every time.

say: I'd keep **lab bills** checked against each practice's appointment records before filing.
I'd use **tested AI notes** only for draft reminders, never final figures.
think: My **junior wage** looks steady under a modest sorter that saves only a little time.
Five months saved cannot prove **retirement affordability** for our household.
do: Match **dental lab invoices** to appointment ledgers before filing.
Ask the **senior reviewer** to explain a mismatched credit note next month.
S0.quote: A missed crown charge is a real person waiting to be paid.
fieldNote: Her occasional **tested AI notes** and source checks are an existing routine, not a new learning tag.
Typical pay, **five months saved** and some nearby firms support calm, though the retirement budget remains unverified.

steps.text: Match dental lab invoices to appointment ledgers before filing
Ask senior reviewer to explain mismatched credit note next month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Lantern to count wrong lab matches before it says the new software saves a review day. The practice owners deserve a wage ledger we can explain, not a faster error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Invoice matching and tax drafting are much of my junior job, so the software could cut my pay even if I learn it. Five months saved means we can look for work, but I would rather keep earning than spend the buffer at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid demonstration of the new matching controls on closed dental files, with a senior checking missed lab bills and repair time; I'd use it on live work only if that test holds. In the first year of steady change, if Lantern cuts my paid week below four days, I'd apply for posted practice billing roles at local dental groups and keep offered Lantern hours until a written wage covering our bills and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours shrinking. I can learn a tested tool, but I cannot make the firm fund the junior rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Lantern offers only unpaid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the approved occasional note tool and ask the partner for a written hours plan. I wouldn't put patient bills into a new system at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the dental group has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid Lantern day still offered and check postings again the next week. A friendly manager's interest is not a written start date.

say: I'd ask for **wrong-match counts** before accepting fewer review hours.
I'd insist on a **named checker** for patient bills.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink under faster matching before I learn the harder tax cases.
Our five-month buffer cannot replace **steady wages** if Lantern cuts a paid day.
do: Learn **matching controls** in paid supervised closed-file practice; use live only after error and repair checks pass.
Apply for **posted practice billing** below four paid days.
Keep **paid Lantern hours** until written bill-covering outside terms begin.
S1.quote: I wouldn't put patient bills into a new system at home.
fieldNote: Her **new tool learning** needs paid supervision and measured errors; refusal returns her to approved note drafting.
A **below-four-day cut** starts a posted search; current pay continues while offered until written bill-covering wage and start.

steps.text: Learn matching controls on paid supervised closed files; use live only after error/repair checks pass
Keep approved note tool and request written hours plan if training unpaid
Apply for posted dental billing if paid week falls below four days
Keep paid Lantern work until written bill-covering outside wage/start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell dental practices that full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking in my tax and billing work before robots reach hands-on clinics around 2031. Standing beside a paper file will not give my accounting desk three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Lantern to lose junior review hours, and my post may end. Arun's market-stall wage and our five months saved would cover some bills, but the missing share of our household income would be hard to rebuild quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd end the paid flower delivery and put its forty-five monthly charge from wages into cash now. In the first year after 2028, if my Lantern post ends, I'd apply for advertised paid invoice-control work at the local medical supplier, keeping any paid Lantern closing files only while offered until a written bill-covering wage, start date and bus-compatible hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a sizeable loss of my own pay. A supplier may still need staff, but its invoice thinking faces AGI in 2028 too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that supplier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dental practices order from it, so I recognise the bills, but I have not been offered a post. I would take only a real salaried vacancy, not unpaid trial days on a warehouse floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bus hours would work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last bus home leaves early enough that a late closing would cost more than the advertised wage suggests. I'd compare the actual shift finish with the timetable before agreeing a written start; I will not assume a lift from Arun.

say: I'd say **2028 billing thinking** changes before 2031 clinic robots.
I'd ask for **real paid vacancies** at the supplier.
think: I expect my **junior review post** could end when AGI reaches tax work.
Arun's **stall wage** cannot replace my whole pay or cover all our bills.
do: Cancel **flower delivery** and save forty-five monthly from wages.
Apply for **posted supplier invoicing** after Lantern job loss.
Keep **offered paid closing files** until written bill-covering pay, start and bus hours are confirmed.
S2.quote: Standing beside a paper file will not give my accounting desk three extra years.
fieldNote: Her **desk work** faces 2028 AGI; a supplier invoice desk is an uncertain paid opening, not a safe physical refuge.
The cancelled delivery adds **new monthly cash**; a move needs a posted paid vacancy, written bill-covering terms and workable bus hours.

steps.text: Cancel flower delivery and save forty-five monthly from wages
Apply for posted paid medical-supplier invoicing after Lantern job loss; require written bill-covering wage/start
Keep paid Lantern closing files while offered until outside start
Accept supplier shifts only if confirmed finish fits last bus home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lantern to use five years to train staff on real errors, not buy certificates with glossy covers. Full AGI reaches the accounts desk in 2031, while robots for physical clinic work follow about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be sixty-three and still need my wage. A medical supplier's office is exposed to AGI as well; knowing its invoices would help me apply, but it would not guarantee a funded post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supplier next spring for four paid supervised invoice-control shifts with Lantern's written paid release, and work them only if both employers approve. In the first year after 2031, if my tax post ends and wages are still needed, I'd apply for a posted paid supplier role only with written bill-covering wage, start date and bus-compatible hours, keeping any paid Lantern work while offered until the outside post begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the need to practise without giving up my current pay. Five years offers time to test the work, but only if somebody funds the shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either employer refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid Lantern accounts work and skip the shifts. I wouldn't use our five-month reserve to work for a supplier for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted paid supplier role if the employer funds the fee and paid study hours. I've a bachelor's degree already; another course has to lead to actual paid work.

say: I'd ask for **paid supervised shifts** on supplier invoices.
I'd explain **2031 desk risk** before 2034 clinic robots.
think: I may still need a **wage at sixty-three** because retirement income is not confirmed.
Supplier billing is **exposed office work**, even if I recognise the invoices.
do: Work **four supervised shifts** only with supplier pay and Lantern’s written paid release; otherwise keep offered paid accounts.
Take a **funded invoice module** only for a posted paid supplier role.
Apply for **posted supplier work** after tax loss if wages remain needed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about securing paid practice.
S3.quote: I wouldn't use our five-month reserve to work for a supplier for free.
fieldNote: The **four-shift trial** is real learning only with both employers' paid approval and supervision; refusal keeps her on paid Lantern work.
The module needs a **posted paid role**, funded fees and paid study time; moving also needs written terms and bus hours.

steps.text: Work four supervised supplier shifts only with supplier pay and Lantern written paid release

Seek posted supplier work after loss if wages needed; require written bill-covering wage/start and bus hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to get actual retirement figures and to judge which dental bills clients still pay us to check. Full AGI reaches my tax desk in 2036, and robots for hands-on clinic work come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight then and might have retired, but that depends on confirmed income and our bills. I will not treat our grown children's wages as a plan, and today's five-month reserve cannot stand in for an unknown pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income estimate and compare it with our bills each autumn while keeping paid Lantern work. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials, I'd stay within that budget; if wages are still needed and Lantern ends my post, I'd apply for posted paid medical-supplier invoicing only with written bill-covering wage, start and bus-compatible hours, retaining any paid Lantern closing files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about income after 2036, but ten years gives us time to verify rather than guess. The supplier might not post a role, so I would keep today's wage while it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire now if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the written figures cover our actual household bills. I like the work, and I won't turn a hope about pension money into a resignation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Lantern still pays you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking dental bills for as long as the firm pays for my hours and the work is there. If those hours end and retirement income is short, I'd search posted paid roles rather than count on a favour from a client. We would use our savings for essentials during that search if paid work ends before adequate retirement income starts.

say: I'd ask for **verified retirement income** before a date.
I'd name **2036 desk risk** before 2039 clinic robots.
think: I might need **wages at sixty-eight** if actual retirement income falls short.

do: Request **written retirement figures** yearly; stay within that budget only if it covers household bills.
Keep **paid Lantern checking** only while offered.
Seek **posted supplier invoicing** if wages needed after 2036 loss; require written bill-covering wage/start and bus-compatible hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about unverified later income.
S4.quote: I'd keep checking dental bills for as long as the firm pays for my hours and the work is there.
fieldNote: Retirement is **conditional on verified income**, with no assumption about a pension amount or grown-child support.
If **wages remain needed**, posted supplier work requires written bill-covering terms and bus-compatible hours; Lantern pay lasts only while offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior invoice desk could end before I know whether retirement income will cover us. Paid supervised supplier shifts and a posted vacancy with written wages, start and workable bus hours would help; an unpaid trial would not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who rings the practice when the lab says an invoice was never paid. The ledger can be neat while the lab technician waits for payment.

headlineQuote: The ledger can be neat while the lab technician waits for payment.
portrait: Bianca, **fifty-eight**, is a junior dental accountant who likes finding credit notes and dislikes repeated chasing.
She has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning tax cases and uses tested AI notes occasionally.
Typical pay, **five months saved** and some local firms give a finite cushion.
She tests new work only with **paid supervised time** and treats supplier billing as exposed desk work.
Retirement needs **verified income**; a wage search continues if AGI ends her post and bills remain.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end her junior post before retirement income is clear.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid supervised shifts** and a posted paid role with written wage, start and bus-compatible hours.
